description: queue (ADR 0031, ADR 0005): the worker's control plane is rows, and the claim protocol is four SQL functions both tiers call — claim_job, heartbeat_job, finish_job, fail_job — all SECURITY INVOKER, so the caller's own role and the transaction's workspace scope are what fence every row they touch. Each suite seeds `workspaces` and `jobs` as the container's superuser (an `enqueued_ago_seconds` and a `lease_expires_in_seconds` are written as instants relative to now, which is how the fixture advances time without waiting), then runs each entry of `claims` as its `role` in its `workspace_id` scope ('' = no scope) and asserts the ids `claim_job` returned, in that order — an empty list meaning zero rows. Every entry of `calls` is then run in the same way and must answer exactly `expect`, and `expect_final` is read back per job as the superuser, `attempts` and `status` together, so a poisoning or a lost lease is visible as the row it left behind.

jobs.why: the oldest queued job in workspace A, so the claim order has something to be older than
claimed by a worker that stopped answering: the lease lapsed, so this job is claimable again and never lost
claimed by a worker that is still answering: its lease has not lapsed, so nothing else may take it
claimed as many times as it may be and lost again: the next claim poisons it rather than spending a fourth attempt on it
another tenant's queued job, which the scope is what keeps out of every claim above

claims.why: the oldest claimable job goes first — which is not the oldest job, because the oldest has spent its attempts and is poisoned by this very claim rather than handed out again
then the next oldest, which is the job whose lease lapsed: a run whose worker died is handed back for another claim rather than lost
and then nothing: a lease somebody is keeping alive is not a job going spare
the app may claim too — the ops command that runs a rebuild in the foreground is a claimant like any other — and in workspace B it takes that tenant's own job
a transaction scoped to no workspace claims nothing at all, which is why none of the four functions needs a workspace argument to guard

calls.why: the claimant's heartbeat keeps its lease
a stranger's heartbeat is refused, so a worker whose lease lapsed cannot push out the lease of whoever replaced it
a stranger's finish is refused too — a run's outcome is written by the run that made it
and a heartbeat from the right worker in the wrong scope reaches no row, because the policy is what the function sees through
the claimant finishes its own job and says what it found
a job is finished once: the second call finds no claimed row to finish
a failure is the claimant's to record, with what went wrong as counts and paths
and a heartbeat after the end is refused, because the lease ended with the job

expect_final.why: failed by its claimant after one claim
the lapsed lease was claimed again — never lost — and finished by its new claimant on its second attempt
the live lease was never touched: still claimed by the worker that is keeping it, on the attempt it was claimed with
poisoned at claim time and never claimed again, so its attempts stand where the last claim left them
the other tenant's job was claimed only from its own scope, and by the app
